summary: Defines the notation used in MIB modules to state the acceptable lower bounds of implementation and the level actually achieved. It is an Internet Standard. It obsoletes RFC 1904.

eli5.summary: This is a way for a maker to say exactly which parts of a standard its product does and does not support.

questions: what is module-compliance in a mib
what is an object group in a mib
subtitle: The notation MIB authors use to say what an SNMP agent must implement, and what a given product actually does.

tldr.problem: A MIB module defines many managed objects, but nothing in the objects themselves says which ones an implementation must support or how a particular product differs from the standard.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2580 defines four ASN.1 macros: OBJECT-GROUP and NOTIFICATION-GROUP bundle related items, MODULE-COMPLIANCE states the minimum a vendor must implement, and AGENT-CAPABILITIES states what a specific agent really implements.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard (STD 58) and obsoletes RFC 1904. It is the conformance part of SMIv2, used alongside RFC 2578 and RFC 2579.

today: RFC 2580 is an Internet Standard (STD 58) and has not been obsoleted. It obsoletes RFC 1904, and it is one of the SMIv2 documents together with RFC 2578 and RFC 2579.

sections.title: Why Conformance Statements Exist
sections.content:
Management information is treated as a collection of managed objects held in a virtual information store called the Management Information Base (MIB). Related objects are grouped into MIB modules, written in an adapted subset of ASN.1 known as the Structure of Management Information (SMI).

It can be useful to define both the acceptable lower bound of an implementation and the level actually achieved. RFC 2580 defines the notation for that. The original SMI is called SMIv1 in this document, and the current version is SMIv2.
sections.eli5: A big list of things a device can report is not much use if nobody knows which ones a device must really support. This RFC gives people a way to write that down.

sections.title: Groups of Objects and Notifications
sections.content:
The OBJECT-GROUP macro defines a collection of related managed objects, and NOTIFICATION-GROUP does the same for notifications. Each has a STATUS of current, deprecated or obsolete, a DESCRIPTION, and an optional REFERENCE. Its value is an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, the name of the group.

Every object in a group must be defined in the same information module as the group, and must have a MAX-ACCESS of accessible-for-notify, read-only, read-write or read-create. Every object in a module with a MAX-ACCESS other than not-accessible must belong to at least one object group. Likewise, every notification must be in at least one notification group. This catches the common mistake of adding an object and forgetting to put it in a group.

To "implement" an object, an agent must return a reasonably accurate value for retrieval, and if the object is writable it must be able to reasonably influence the underlying managed entity. An agent must never return a value for an object it does not implement; it must return the appropriate exception or error, such as noSuchObject. A group by itself carries no conformance information. That comes from including it in a compliance statement.
sections.eli5: A group is a labelled bag of related items. Every item must go into some bag, so none gets forgotten, and a device must never pretend to have an item it does not have.

sections.title: Compliance Statements
sections.content:
The MODULE-COMPLIANCE macro states the minimum requirements for implementing one or more MIB modules. Every standard MIB module must have a corresponding MODULE-COMPLIANCE specification, either in the same module or in a companion one.

A MODULE clause names each module covered. Inside it:

  • MANDATORY-GROUPS lists groups that are unconditionally required. An agent claiming compliance must implement every object and notification in them.
  • GROUP names groups that are conditionally mandatory (for example, only if a certain protocol is implemented) or unconditionally optional. Its DESCRIPTION says under what conditions it is required.
  • OBJECT refines the requirement for a single object, using SYNTAX, WRITE-SYNTAX and MIN-ACCESS.

A group named in neither MANDATORY-GROUPS nor a GROUP clause is unconditionally optional. An implementation complies on access when what it offers is at least the MIN-ACCESS level and at most the MAX-ACCESS of the object's OBJECT-TYPE.
sections.eli5: The compliance statement is the rule sheet. Some bags are must-bring, some are bring-only-if-you-play-a-certain-game, and the rest are optional.

sections.title: Agent Capabilities Statements
sections.content:
The AGENT-CAPABILITIES macro lets an agent implementor describe the precise level of support an agent claims, and bind that description to the value of an instance of sysORID. A management station can keep a database of these statements, read the sysORID values from an agent, look up the matching entries and tune its behavior to that agent.

Each SUPPORTS clause names a MIB module, followed by an INCLUDES clause listing the groups the agent implements. Optional VARIATION clauses then record where an object or notification differs from its definition. A variation can refine SYNTAX or WRITE-SYNTAX, lower the ACCESS (the value not-implemented means the item is absent), name CREATION-REQUIRES objects for row creation, or give an alternate DEFVAL. Every VARIATION needs a DESCRIPTION.

The macro describes variations against OBJECT-TYPE and NOTIFICATION-TYPE definitions, not against MODULE-COMPLIANCE statements. The RFC also suggests listing enumerated objects explicitly in a VARIATION, because later revisions of a module may add enumerations.
sections.eli5: If the compliance statement is the rule sheet, the capabilities statement is one kid's honest report: "I brought these bags, but this one toy is missing and that one only half works."

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives one usage example per macro. The snmpGroup object group lists 7 objects, and snmpBasicNotificationsGroup lists the 2 notifications an agent is required to implement, coldStart and authenticationFailure.

A hypothetical xyzMIBCompliance requires five mandatory groups, plus the xyzV1Group only for entities that also implement XYZv1.

The exampleAgent capabilities statement describes an "ACME Agent release 1.1 for 4BSD" supporting six MIB modules. It records, for instance, that ipInAddrErrors is not-implemented and that tcpConnState is read-only.
sections.eli5: The examples show filled-in versions of each form, so you can see what a real checklist and a real honest report look like.

sections.title: Revising Groups and Statements
sections.content:
Groups, compliance definitions and capabilities definitions can be referenced elsewhere, so changes that would alter what an existing reference means are not allowed. Such changes need a new definition with a new descriptor and a new OBJECT IDENTIFIER value.

Allowed revisions are: moving STATUS from current to deprecated or obsolete (and deprecated to obsolete), with the DESCRIPTION updated to explain why; adding or updating a REFERENCE; clarifying the DESCRIPTION; and any editorial change. For AGENT-CAPABILITIES, STATUS may only move from current to obsolete, because that macro has no deprecated value.
sections.eli5: Once a rule sheet is handed out, you cannot quietly change what it means. If the rules really change, you write a new sheet with a new name.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that defining conformance requirements this way has no security impact on the Internet. The macros only describe what should be implemented, and their expansion conceptually happens during implementation, not at run-time.
sections.eli5: These are only paperwork lists, so they do not open any new doors for trouble.

viz.caption: THE FOUR MACROS DEFINED BY RFC 2580

items.title: OBJECT-GROUP
items.text: A named collection of related managed objects.

items.title: NOTIFICATION-GROUP
items.text: A named collection of related notifications.

items.title: MODULE-COMPLIANCE
items.text: The minimum a vendor must implement for one or more MIB modules.

items.title: AGENT-CAPABILITIES
items.text: What a specific agent actually supports, including variations.

viz.caption: OBJECT GROUP EXAMPLE FROM THE RFC (SECTION 3.6)

data.title: snmpGroup
data.code:
snmpGroup OBJECT-GROUP
    OBJECTS { snmpInPkts,
              snmpInBadVersions,
              snmpInASNParseErrs,
              snmpBadOperations,
              snmpSilentDrops,
              snmpProxyDrops,
              snmpEnableAuthenTraps }
    STATUS  current
    DESCRIPTION
            "A collection of objects providing basic instrumentation
            and control of an agent."
   ::= { snmpMIBGroups 8 }
